newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bonn backs jobs, rejects monetary meddling.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bonn backs jobs, rejects monetary meddling.

text.p: The German government on Thursday firmly rejected any notion of reopening a controversial debate over whether to set up a political counterweight to the future European central bank with the aim of boosting jobs and growth.

Bonn has bowed to pressure from the new Socialist-led French government and agreed to back inclusion of an Employment Chapter in the Maastricht II treaty to be discussed at a European Union summit in Amsterdam on June 16-17.

But, under pressure not to bend too far, the finance ministry made clear that Germany was not about to support a previous French proposal for an "economic government" which Bonn fears could meddle with monetary policy decisions.
"There is no need for a counterweight to the European central bank," said a finance ministry spokeswoman. "Monetary stability must not become a matter of politics."

In remarks to reporters on Thursday the leader of the main opposition Social Democrats (SPD) Oskar Lafontaine said he supported France's demand to create a 'European economic government' to offset the planned independent central bank.
"Politicians can make mistakes -- but so can institutions which are apparently independent," he said.
Separately, the Dutch government, currently holding the rotating European Union presidency, presented a draft for the Employment Chapter, which it said reflected German concerns.
According to the draft, EU leaders would be able to approve by majority vote coordinated measures to boost economic growth and jobs as long as this did not incur large spending.
But concern is running high that this is the first step towards giving Brussels a blank check for jobs programmes.
Manfred Neumann, head of the economics ministry's advisory panel, urged Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt to block any plans to tranfer such policy authority to Brussels.
"I fear that it is going to come to this," he said. "And once they have the power, then you can forget everything else. There is no need for Brussels to start its own initiatives."

Concerns that Germany, an advocate of strict fiscal discipline in the run-up to monetary union, could soften its position have risen since a row between Bonn and the Bundesbank over plans to revalue reserves to plug budget deficits.
The debate seriously shook financial market confidence in Germany's preparations for monetary union and offered a rare view of the central bank's power in guiding economic policy.

The Bundesbank, meeting on Thursday for the first time since the dispute broke out, said it expected to soon hammer out final details of a compromise with Finance Minister Theo Waigel on the plan, ending a painful chapter in its relations with Bonn.
"Based on the results of talks so far the central bank council sees good prospects for a solution which takes account of the fundamental position it outlined in its statement on May 28," it said.
But concern is still high Germany's difficulty meeting the tough fiscal criteria for entry into monetary union in 1999 could lead it to agree to a watering down of the targets.

Edmund Stoiber, the Euro-sceptical Bavarian state premier, said in an interview with ZDF public television that Germany's Constitutional Court has already ruled that the Maastricht criteria must be strictly observed or Germany cannot join.
"If the criteria are exceeded and it cannot be prevented politically, then in the end the Constitutional Court will make the final decision," Stoiber said.

Gerhard Schroeder, SPD premier of Lower Saxony and a strong challenger to Chancellor Helmut Kohl, made similar comments, saying he would prefer delaying monetary union if the criteria could not be met and denied that a delay would be a disaster.
"I just cannot believe the catastrophic scenarios as they are being portrayed," he said. "European integration sometimes moves ahead quickly, sometimes slowly."
Opinion polls show Germans are still fearful of EMU.
Almost half the German population fears Europe's planned single currency because of worries the euro will be worth less than the mark, the Wickert Institute said.
Those fearing EMU said the euro would be a "devalued" currency (51 percent), "purchasing power would be diminished" (15 percent) and the project "lacks transparency" (13 percent).
Fifty-four percent of Germans surveyed in the respected Allensbach Institute's latest monthly poll said they expected monetary union to start on time even though 52 percent said they were against it.
